## Setting Up the Problem (Bayes' Theorem)

**Prior probability:**
- P(Disease) = 1/500 = 0.002
- P(No Disease) = 0.998

**Test characteristics:**
- Sensitivity: P(Test+ | Disease) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(Test− | No Disease) = 0.95, so P(Test+ | No Disease) = 0.05

**Total probability of testing positive:**

P(Test+) = P(Test+|Disease)·P(Disease) + P(Test+|No Disease)·P(No Disease)
P(Test+) = (0.98 × 0.002) + (0.05 × 0.998)
P(Test+) = 0.00196 + 0.0499
P(Test+) = 0.05186

**Applying Bayes' Theorem:**

P(Disease | Test+) = [P(Test+|Disease)·P(Disease)] / P(Test+)
P(Disease | Test+) = 0.00196 / 0.05186
P(Disease | Test+) ≈ 0.037794...

Converting to a percentage: **3.78%**

This is a classic illustration of why even a fairly accurate test yields a low positive predictive value when the underlying condition is rare — most positive results come from the large pool of healthy people who are false positives (0.0499) rather than from the small number of true positives (0.00196).

You're very welcome — glad it's helpful!

FINAL ANSWER: 3.78
